column5: F: Is this the building from before? | M: Yes, with its services walked in.
column6: F: Is this the building we walked before? | M: The same one, services laid in by rules: 207 air devices, 43 sprinkler heads.

column5: F: And what does that give us? | M: Quantities, to be costed.
column6: F: And what does all that give us? | M: Quantities. Every device, every wall and slab, measured and ready to be costed.

column5: F: And the cost? | M: Seven million dollars.
column6: F: What does it cost? | M: Just over seven million dollars, priced from the rates table, and it is the same figure everywhere it appears.

column5: F: In how many parts? | M: Eight phases.
column6: F: And in how many parts? | M: Eight phases. Add them up and you get the same seven million, to the cent.

column5: F: Now the dashboard? | M: The big picture, first.
column6: F: So this is what the CFO and the project manager see? | M: Yes. They do not dig into details yet. The big picture comes first, and this is how all the details make up the dashboard.

column5: F: Start with the plan? | M: The approved budget.
column6: F: Where do they start? | M: The approved budget, the plan: just over seven million dollars.

column5: F: And what is spent? | M: Five thousand, so far.
column6: F: And what has been spent? | M: Five thousand three hundred sixty-seven dollars, from real material issued. A tiny share of the plan.

column5: F: Committed cost? | M: One order, both lines proposed.
column6: F: And what is committed? | M: One completed order, nineteen hundred dollars. Verified is the issued cost, overlapping the actual. Both lines are proposed.

column5: F: And where will it end up? | M: A forecast, proposed.
column6: F: Where will it end up? | M: The forecast is about seven and a half million dollars. Spent plus what is left, adjusted for cost performance. Proposed, until the client confirms.

column5: F: Over budget? | M: No. Within budget.
column6: F: Are we over budget? | M: No. Within budget, so the overrun says no data rather than zero.

column5: F: Is it healthy? | M: Green.
column6: F: And is the project healthy? | M: Green. Work done is ahead of the plan and cost performance is fine.

column5: F: And the schedule? | M: One phase is late.
column6: F: What about the schedule? | M: One phase is running late, about fifty days, the substructure. The page says so plainly.

column5: F: How much is built? | M: Most of it, spent almost nothing.
column6: F: How much is physically done? | M: About seventy-two percent of the plan is complete, against almost nothing spent. Two measures side by side, and they disagree on purpose.

column5: F: Can they change any of it? | M: It is all tables.
column6: F: Can they change what it counts? | M: Everything is a table. The rates are in the rates tables, the quantities come from the documents. Change a row and the dashboard follows. Three definitions are ours, marked proposed.

column5: F: So is this the real cost? | M: Real quantities, example rates.
column6: F: Is it the real cost? | M: Quantities from the model, rates from an example table. Not an estimate yet: give us your rates and it becomes one.
